summary: Describes how the Domain Name System can store data tied to E.164 telephone numbers and resolve those numbers into URIs that can be used in call setup. It also covers identifying services associated with a number. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 3761.

eli5.summary: The internet phone book normally maps names to addresses. Here you look up a regular telephone number and learn how to reach that person over the internet.

subtitle: How a telephone number becomes a DNS name, and DNS records turn that name into URIs for reaching the person.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers in the E.164 format have no built-in way to find internet services such as SIP or email addresses for the same subscriber.
tldr.mechanism: ENUM turns an E.164 number into a domain name under e164.arpa by reversing its digits, then looks up NAPTR records in the DNS. Records that carry the E2U service field yield URIs, and non-terminal records can point on to another domain.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3761 and mostly adds clarifications, collected from deployment experience, to fix interoperability problems between clients and provisioning systems.

today: RFC 6116 is a Proposed Standard and obsoletes RFC 3761. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it, per the metadata for this unit.

sections.title: Telephone Numbers in the DNS
sections.content:
ENUM uses the Domain Name System (DNS) to store data tied to E.164 numbers and to resolve them into URIs that can be used, for example, in telephony call setup. It also lets the DNS identify the services tied to a number. E.164 is the ITU format for international public telephone numbers.

It is a Dynamic Delegation Discovery System (DDDS) Application. The number is changed into a DNS name, and standard DNS features such as NS delegation and NAPTR queries do the lookup. This keeps the usual DNS decentralized control of each level.

The domain e164.arpa is assigned for this data and divided into subdomains. Number holders who want a listing contact the zone administrator named in the zone policy, found starting from the zone's SOA record. Policies can differ in different parts of the world.
sections.eli5: Think of turning your phone number into a special address in the internet phone book, then reading what is written there about how to reach you.

sections.title: From Number to Domain Name
sections.content:
The Application Unique String (AUS) is the full E.164 number with every non-digit removed except the leading +. For example, +44-116-496-0348 becomes +441164960348.

The First Well Known Rule turns the AUS into a key, which for ENUM is a fully qualified domain name:

  1. Remove all characters except digits, which drops the +.
  2. Reverse the order of the digits.
  3. Put a dot between each digit.
  4. Append .e164.arpa..

That name is queried for NAPTR records. A record whose flags field is empty produces a new domain name to query. The output of the last loop is an absolute URI. The algorithm always returns a single rule, though applications may present several results.
sections.eli5: Write your phone number backwards, put a dot between each digit, and add .e164.arpa at the end. That is where the phone book keeps your page.

sections.title: NAPTR Records, Flags and Services
sections.content:
The only database defined for ENUM is the NAPTR DNS record from RFC 3403. The flags field signals when the algorithm is finished. Only one flag, U, is defined: this rule is the last one and its output is a URI. A client that sees an unknown flag MUST ignore that record. With no flag, the rule is non-terminal, its result MUST be a domain name, and the client queries it for more NAPTR records.

The Services field of a terminal record is the literal E2U followed by one or more Enumservices, each introduced by +. An Enumservice is a type with optional :subtype parts, each 1 to 32 characters of letters, digits or hyphen. E2U marks ENUM-only rewrite rules to avoid collisions. A compound NAPTR such as E2U+voice:tel+sms:tel holds several Enumservices that share one URI and are treated as left-to-right priority.

Enumservices are registered under RFC 6117. Types starting with X- are experimental and not registrable. Types starting with P- are for private networks only, will not be registered, MUST NOT be provisioned in systems answering outside queries, and clients MUST discard them unless sure they are on that private network.
sections.eli5: Each entry in the phone book either says here is the final contact, or go look on that other page. The final entries also say what kind of contact it is, like voice or email.

sections.title: An ENUM Example
sections.content:
The RFC's example gives three terminal NAPTR records for one number. The first, with priority 50, produces a SIP URI. The second, with priority 51, produces an H.323 URI. The third, with priority 52, produces a mailto URI. The domain is therefore preferably contacted by SIP, secondly by H.323 for voice, and thirdly by SMTP for messaging.

The Enumservice tokens sip, h323 and email are registered with IANA but have no implicit connection to the protocols or URI schemes of the same names. The first two records match only the number +441632960083; the last matches any value. After ENUM, the next step is to use the resolution mechanism of each URI scheme to find the node to contact.
sections.eli5: One person lists three ways to be reached, in order of preference: a net phone call, another call type, and email. You try them from the top.

sections.title: Interoperability Rules for Provisioning and Clients
sections.content:
Because DDDS is flexible, implementations interpreted it differently. This section, based on the analysis in RFC 5483, sets rules so clients and provisioning systems work together.

Provisioning. NAPTRs SHOULD stay in printable US-ASCII, use 100 as the default ORDER, use ! as the Regexp delimiter, and avoid the i flag. A literal + in the expression MUST be escaped as \+. Zones MUST NOT use the obsolete RFC 2916 syntax. A non-terminal NAPTR MUST carry its target in the Replacement field, with an empty Regexp field. Non-terminals SHOULD NOT be provisioned unless all clients can process them, and no more than 5 should be processed in one query.

Clients. They MUST sort records with ORDER as the major key and PREFERENCE as the minor key, lowest first, and SHOULD NOT discard a record until it is considered or an earlier one is accepted. ORDER applies only within one record set. A discarded record SHOULD NOT end the whole query. Clients MUST handle other delimiters, complex patterns, and an empty Flags field without failure, and SHOULD discard records with other than 3 unescaped delimiters. They MUST detect referential loops, and MAY treat a chain of more than 5 non-terminal NAPTRs as a loop.
sections.eli5: A phone book only works if the people who write entries and the people who read them follow the same rules. This section lists those rules, such as how to order entries and what to do when an entry looks odd.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ENUM relies on DNS, which in its current form cannot prove that the data is authentic, so attacking the DNS is one way of attacking ENUM. A deployed ENUM service SHOULD include mitigations, and most threats can be addressed by verifying data with DNSSEC (RFC 4033). Denial of service cannot be solved that way, and the threat covers not only NAPTR lookups but also records such as NS, MX, SRV and A. Even with DNSSEC, a service SHOULD authenticate the entity it connects to rather than trust a retrieved address.

Caching can make the chain of records, from the E2U NAPTR through to an IP address, inconsistent while changes propagate, so provisioners should minimize changes. Where several providers offer call routing, systems that let users change routing information need identification, authentication and authorization of change requests. Security issues of each URI belong in its Enumservice registration.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks a wrong entry into the phone book, you might call the wrong place. So check who you reach, not just the number you were given.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 3761
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 3761. Its main addition is the section on how DDDS is used in ENUM, collected from deployment experience, with many clarifications to ease interoperability. These include a default ORDER value and Regexp delimiter, required use of the Replacement field in non-terminal NAPTRs, and case-insensitive string matching (Section 3.6).

It also removes the discussion of registration mechanisms, now in RFC 6117, fixes an error by allowing a hyphen in the type and subtype fields, and adds the P- private service type. It also forbids using the term ENUM for these techniques on dialing plans or other digit strings, which must not use e164.arpa and should use an AUS without the leading +.
sections.eli5: This is the improved edition of an earlier rulebook. It fixes mix-ups people ran into and moves one topic to another document.
